say: Good morning, inquirers! Today everything turns: you, the hands of a clock, and a robot. An angle tells us how much something has turned.
Remember: notice it, test it with a protractor or a paper clock, explain why.
Everybody stand up and face the front. The front is North. Ready? Quarter turn clockwise! Which way are you facing now?
Back to North. Half turn! Now 45 degrees anticlockwise: just half of a quarter turn. Where are you facing?
On a clock, which o’clock times do you think make a right angle between the hands? Write down your guess before you try.
stuck: Stuck: put the minute hand on 12. Move only the hour hand, one number at a time.
Not sure if it is a right angle: hold the corner of a square of paper between the hands.
Finished early: what is the angle at 1 o’clock? How can you work it out without a protractor?

say: “I estimate first. This angle is a bit smaller than a right angle, so about 60 or 70 degrees. I put the centre of the protractor on the vertex and the baseline along one arm. That arm points to 0 on the inside scale, so I count up the inside scale: 10, 20 … 65. Not 115: my estimate says it is smaller than 90.”

“A clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees, cut into 12 equal spaces. 360 divided by 12 is 30. At 2 o’clock the hands are 2 spaces apart: 60 degrees. At 10 o’clock I go the shorter way: also 2 spaces, 60 degrees.”
“I face North-West. I turn 135 degrees clockwise. Each step on the compass is 45 degrees, so 135 is 3 steps: North, North-East, East. I face East.”

do: Ask: “Is this angle bigger or smaller than a right angle? So which number on the protractor makes sense?”
Ask: “How many spaces apart are the hands? How many degrees is one space?”
Ask: “How many 45° steps is that turn? Which way: clockwise or anticlockwise?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Estimate first: compare with the corner of a page (90°).”
Hint 2: “Draw the clock or the compass and count the spaces or steps with your pencil.”
Hint 3: “For a corner of a square or rectangle: the parts add up to 90°. Take away the parts you know.”

say: “Is turning 270° clockwise the same as turning 90° anticlockwise? Test it: stand up and do both.”
“Ben says the angle at 3 o’clock is smaller than at 9 o’clock because 3 is smaller than 9. Who agrees?”
ask: “Is turning 270° clockwise the same as turning 90° anticlockwise? Test it: stand up and do both.”

Yes: 270° clockwise and 90° anticlockwise make a full turn (360°) together, so you end up facing the same way. Ben is wrong: at 3 o’clock and at 9 o’clock the hands are 3 spaces apart the shorter way, so both angles are 90°.

say: “Today you estimated before you measured, counted spaces on a clock and steps on a compass, and found every angle in a fan. Inquirers check with an estimate. Well done!”

p4l6-title.note: Objective: Estimate and measure angles with a protractor, find every angle in a fan of rays, work out angles between clock hands (30° for each space) and turns of the minute hand (6° a minute), turn on the 8-point compass (45° steps) and work backwards from a turn, and find unknown angles in squares and rectangles. Thinking strategies today: ESTIMATE FIRST (compare with 90° and 180°), COUNT THE TURN (12 clock spaces, 8 compass steps), WORK IN ORDER (every angle in a fan), WORK BACKWARDS (undo a turn). Materials: A clear 180° protractor and a 30 cm ruler for each child (not printed in the kit: families bring one from home; keep two or three spares), a paper clock with a split pin (or a real clock), a square of paper for checking right angles, mini whiteboards, a compass card on the floor or wall. Online: children use their own protractor and a paper clock at home; the screen is North for the turning games, and children stand and turn on camera. Time plan: opening 0 to 1, sneak-peek puzzles 1 to 4 (two ideas we have not learnt yet; answers shown to the tutor only, on camera, nobody marked), warm-up game 4 to 6 (one short round), quick questions 6 to 8, explore 8 to 18 (a Go further what-if is on the slide from minute 8), teaching 18 to 30 (click to reveal each step and answer; the "your turn" slides are optional, skip them if short of time), brain break 30 to 34, worksheet page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 36 to 50 (after the 2-minute protractor demo at 34 to 36) and check together 50 to 53, short teaching before page 2 53 to 58, worksheet page 2 (on your own) 58 to 76 and check together 76 to 80, talk time 80 to 85, exit ticket 85 to 88, looking back (reflection) 88 to 90 (2 minutes). After question 3 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children).

p4l6-check.note: Minutes 1 to 4 (3 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. About 90 seconds each. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and held to the camera at the same moment for everyone (or shown only to you on camera). Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards up in front of the group, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Ask for volunteers first if you want a reason said aloud; nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 2 quarter turns, which is a half turn. You are facing the opposite way (your back is to the screen). 2) 55°. A square corner is 90°, and 90° − 35° = 55°. A GOOD REASON: A square corner is 90° and a half turn is 180°. Angles side by side add up to the whole turn. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. After question 3 on page 1 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l6-warm1.note: Minutes 4 to 6 (one short round, about 2 minutes: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Robot turns. Everyone stands and faces the front of the room: that is North (online: the screen is North). Read each call; children turn, then point and say the direction they face. Click to show it. Start every call from North. Then play faster rounds without the slide: "From where you are now: quarter turn anticlockwise! Half turn! 45° clockwise!" Children who end up facing the wrong way watch a partner and try again. Ask: "How many quarter turns make a full turn?" (4) "How many 45° turns make a quarter turn?" (2) "Is a half turn clockwise different from a half turn anticlockwise?" (no: you end up facing the same way). Listen for children who say "clockwise is the way the clock hands go". Online: on a mirrored self-view a turn looks reversed, so say "turn to your right" for clockwise, and tell children to ignore their own picture.

p4l6-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Whiteboards up together, then click. 1) 90°. 2) 180°: two right angles. 3) 4, so a full turn is 4 × 90° = 360°. 4) W: stand up and do it if anyone hesitates. 5) A 3/4 turn is 3 × 90° = 270°, which is more than 250°. Ask: "How many degrees in a 1/4 turn? A 1/8 turn?" (90°, 45°: we need 45° today for the compass).

p4l6-explore1.note: Minutes 8 to 13. Pairs use a paper clock (online: a paper clock at home or a real clock held to the camera). Ask them to predict first: which times make a right angle? Most children say 3 o’clock; fewer think of 9 o’clock. They check each time with the corner of a square of paper. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: what is the angle at 1 o’clock? At 2 o’clock? Can you work it out without a protractor? GO FURTHER (on the slide from minute 8, so nobody waits): What if the clock shows half past three (3:30)? Is the angle still 90°? Why not? Answer: No. It is 75°: at 3:30 the hour hand has moved halfway from 3 to 4, which is 15° past the 3. The minute hand points at 6 (180°) and the hour hand at 105°.

p4l6-explore2.note: Minutes 13 to 18. Gather the pairs. Answers: 1) 3 o’clock and 9 o’clock (3 spaces apart either way). 2) 6 o’clock: a straight line, a half turn, 180°. 3) 30°: a full turn is 360° and the clock face has 12 equal spaces, so 360 ÷ 12 = 30. Check: 3 o’clock is 3 spaces, 3 × 30 = 90 ✓. Many children say 12 o’clock is a straight line too: the hands are on top of each other, so the angle is 0°. Keep the 30° idea: we use it after the break.

p4l6-teach1.note: Teach. Hold up a real protractor. Ask first: "Is this angle bigger or smaller than a right angle?" (smaller: estimate about 60°). Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "The bottom arm points to 0 on the INSIDE scale, so I count up the inside scale: 10, 20 … 60, 65. The outside scale says 115 at the same place, but 115 is more than a right angle and my estimate says less. So the angle is 65°." Online: children measure the angle on their screen with a real protractor if the screen is large enough, or on the worksheet later. Point out: the length of the arms does not change the angle.

p4l6-try1.note: Whiteboards: children write an estimate for each before you click. Benchmarks: a right angle is 90°, a straight line is 180°, half a right angle is 45°. A is less than half a right angle: about 30°. B is just more than a right angle: about 100°. C is between a right angle and a straight line, nearer the straight line: about 145°. They measure with a protractor on the worksheet; here we only estimate. Estimates within 15° are good.

p4l6-teach2.note: Teach. Children stand facing the front (North) and act it out. Think-aloud: "I face North-West. Each step on the compass is 45 degrees, so 135 degrees is 3 steps. Clockwise is the way clock hands go: North, North-East, East. I face East." Common mistake: counting NW itself as the first step. Point with a finger: move first, then count. Then the second example: 225° is 5 steps; anticlockwise from E: NE, N, NW, W, SW. Ask: "What turn would get back from SW to E?" (225° clockwise, or 135° anticlockwise, the shorter way).

p4l6-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 1 step: NE. b) A 3/4 turn is 270° = 6 steps clockwise from S: SW, W, NW, N, NE, E. Or think: 3/4 clockwise is the same as 1/4 anticlockwise, and 1/4 anticlockwise from S is E. c) Clockwise from E to NW is 5 steps (225°); anticlockwise is 3 steps (135°), so the smallest turn is 135° anticlockwise.

p4l6-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Reading the wrong protractor scale (40° written as 140°) instead of starting from the 0 on the arm and checking with an estimate. (2) Counting the numbers on the clock instead of the spaces between them, or measuring the bigger way round (210° instead of 150° at 7 o’clock). (3) Compass turns: mixing up clockwise and anticlockwise, or counting the starting direction as the first 45° step.

p4l6-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stand in view of the camera; the screen is North. Finish with "Turn to face the screen" from different directions: who turned the smallest way?

p4l6-teachfan.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q2 has 4 rays). Online: many cameras show a mirrored self-view, so left and right can look swapped when a child shows a paper protractor or points an arm; check against the shared slide, not the video tile. Name angles with three letters: the middle letter is always the vertex O. Think-aloud: "First the small angles that sit next to each other: 20° and 50°. Then two together: 20 + 50 = 70°. With 3 rays there are 3 angles." Do NOT give the number of angles for 4 rays: let pairs find it on the worksheet. Hint for strugglers: "Start from OA. List every angle that starts at OA, then every angle that starts at OB …"

p4l6-ws1.note: Minutes 36 to 50. Walk around and watch protractors: centre on the vertex, baseline on an arm, count from 0. Ask "Does your answer match your estimate?" Q1c and d are turned, so children must turn the protractor (or the page). Accept answers within 2°. CHOOSING: after question 3 every child may carry on or try the Think harder page. Invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l6-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1: accept 2° either way. If a child wrote 140° for a, ask "Is a bigger than a right angle?" Q2: work in order. Small angles: ∠AOB 30°, ∠BOC 60°, ∠COD 45°. Two together: ∠AOC = 30 + 60 = 90°, ∠BOD = 60 + 45 = 105°. All three: ∠AOD = 30 + 60 + 45 = 135°. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 angles.

p4l6-teachclock.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3). Link back to explore: 3 o’clock was 90° = 3 spaces, so one space is 30°. Click 1: 2 o’clock. Click 2 shows 10 o’clock: "Is it 10 spaces? No: go the shorter way, from 10 to 12, 2 spaces." Then the minute hand: it goes all the way round (360°) in 60 minutes, so 360 ÷ 60 = 6° a minute, or 30° every 5 minutes. Count on with a paper clock: 6:05 to 6:20 is 3 jumps of 5 minutes, 3 × 30° = 90°.

p4l6-tryclock.note: Whiteboards. a) From 9 to 12 is 3 spaces: 90°. b) 6 spaces: 180°, a straight line. c) 40 minutes × 6° = 240°, or 8 jumps of 5 minutes × 30°. Note: c is more than a half turn; that is fine for a turn of the hand.

p4l6-teachrect.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 has two parts; the third drawing, two squares, is an optional extension and is the idea behind Go further 9). Fold a square of paper to show the corner is a right angle. Click each answer after children try on whiteboards. Rectangle: the whole corner is 90°, so the missing part is 90 − 37 = 53°. Square cut in three: 90 − 20 − 45 = 25° (check 20 + 25 + 45 = 90). Two squares: the two right angles together make 180°, but the overlap of 40° is counted twice, so 180 − 40 = 140°. Act it out with two paper squares on top of each other.

p4l6-teachrobot.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4d works backwards; Q6a is the robot). Act it out: one child is the robot, the group reads the cards. To undo a turn, turn the same amount the other way, like taking off shoes after socks. Check Mei: start E, 90° clockwise is S ✓. For "find all pairs" (a Think harder question now): with three cards A, B, C the pairs are A and B, A and C, B and C. Example (not on the worksheet): cards 45° clockwise, 90° anticlockwise, 180°, from N to E. 45 + 180: SW, not this one. 45 cw and 90 acw: NW, not this one. 90 acw and 180: E ✓. Only one pair works.

p4l6-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially anyone who still counts the starting direction as a step or counts the numbers on the clock instead of the spaces. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q3 and Q4 first. Q5 and Q6 are choices for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which.

p4l6-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3b: 7 o’clock is 5 spaces the shorter way (7 to 12), 150°, not 210°. The minute-hand question (3:10 to 3:35 is 25 minutes × 6° = 150°) is now a Think harder item, so the page has fewer parts. Q4b: 135° is 3 steps anticlockwise from SW: S, SE, E. Q4c: clockwise NE, E, SE, S is 3 steps (135°); anticlockwise would be 5 steps (225°). Q4d: undo 90° anticlockwise by turning 90° clockwise from NW: N, NE. Q5: 90 − 58 = 32; 90 − 15 − 48 = 27. (The overlapping-squares idea is now a Go further question.) Q6a: N → E → NE → SW. The "find ALL the pairs" question is now Think harder stretch 4: list all 6 pairs: 45+90 (SE), 45 cw + 135 acw (W ✓), 45+180 (SW), 90 cw + 135 acw (NW), 90+180 (W ✓), 135 acw + 180 (NE).

p4l6-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) N (225° is 5 steps of 45°: S, SW, W, NW, N) 2) 60° and 60°. Both are 2 spaces apart the shorter way. 3) 210° (35 minutes × 6°) 4) Two ways: 45° clockwise and 135° anticlockwise; or 90° clockwise and 180°.

p4l6-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 75°. At 3:30 the minute hand points to 6, but the hour hand is HALFWAY between 3 and 4 (half an hour has passed). From the hour hand to 4 is half a space (15°), from 4 to 6 is 2 spaces (60°): 75°. 2) 10 angles (4 small, 3 of two parts, 2 of three parts, 1 of four parts). Each small angle is 120 ÷ 4 = 30°, so the three-part angles are 90°: 2 right angles. More are in the question bank and on the Think harder pages.

p4l6-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Q1, is the hour hand pointing exactly at 3? Why not? How far has it moved since 3 o’clock? Q2, how big is each small angle? How can you count the angles without missing one? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l6-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: many children say 90°, as if the hour hand still pointed at 3. Use a real clock: move the minute hand from 12 to 6 and watch the hour hand creep half way to 4. Q2: the list in order (by number of parts) is the same idea as the fan on page 1; 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 is a pattern worth noticing: with 6 rays it would be 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15.

p4l6-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 85. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then test it standing up: everyone faces North and does both turns. Answer: yes, you end up facing the same way (both from N end at W), because 270° + 90° = 360°, a full turn. The turns are different sizes, but the direction you end up facing is the same. Second question if time: "Ben says the angle at 3 o’clock is smaller than at 9 o’clock because 3 is smaller than 9. Who agrees?" (both are 90°: 3 spaces the shorter way). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake.

p4l6-exit.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Answers: SE (3 steps of 45°: NE, E, SE). 150° (5 spaces of 30°). Extension: find all the o’clock times when the smaller angle between the hands is more than 90° (4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 o’clock).

p4l6-reflect.note: Minutes 88 to 90 (2 minutes). LOOKING BACK. Children fill in the box on the Investigation page, the page every child has (something I did well; the hardest part was; what helped me; one thing I could try next). Say: "You can write, tick or pass. Ticking I am still stuck is a good thing to do: it tells me where to help." Model one yourself first: "Something I did well: I estimated each angle before I measured. The hardest part was reading the protractor scale. What helped me: starting from the 0 that lines up with one arm. One thing I could try next: checking my estimate before I read the protractor." Do not ask anyone to read theirs out. If a child wants to share, take one volunteer and thank them for the strategy. Never grade it, never correct it, never collect it for marks and never show it to the group. You may look at a child's page only when the child holds it to your camera. Never ask for photos or private messages. If I am still stuck is ticked, check in during the open session: a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never send a DM. Praise strategies ("you drew it", "you asked for help"), not speed or scores.
